passages.happening:
The turn of the whole story comes in one sentence: “But God remembered Noah and all the animals and livestock that were with him in the ark” (verse 1).

God sends a wind over the earth, and the waters begin to go down. The springs of the deep and the floodgates of the heavens are closed. The rain stops (verse 2). After 150 days the waters have fallen (verse 3).

“On the seventeenth day of the seventh month, the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat” (verse 4). The waters keep going down, and on the first day of the tenth month the tops of the mountains can be seen (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
When the Bible says God ‘remembered’, it does not mean he had forgotten. It means he acted, out of faithfulness, for someone he was bound to. Later God ‘remembered’ Rachel and gave her a child (Genesis 30:22). He ‘remembered’ his covenant and rescued Israel from Egypt (Exodus 2:24). Here his remembering turns the story from judgment to rescue. And notice who he remembers: Noah and the animals. Even the livestock are not forgotten.

The word for ‘wind’ is ruach, the same word as the ‘Spirit’ of God hovering over the waters in 1:2. As at the beginning, God's wind moves over the waters, and dry land will appear. The flood is creation run backward; now creation begins again.

‘Came to rest’ is a word that sounds like Noah's name (nuach, rest). The boy named for rest (5:29) comes to rest at last.

‘The mountains of Ararat’ is plural. It names a region, not one peak. Ararat is the land that Assyrian writings call Urartu, the mountain country around Lake Van, in what is now eastern Turkey and Armenia. The peak called Mount Ararat today got that name much later. Claims to have found the ark there have never been confirmed.
passages.later:
Ararat appears again in the Bible as a far northern land. Sennacherib's sons “escaped to the land of Ararat” after killing their father (2 Kings 19:37), and Jeremiah names it among distant kingdoms (Jeremiah 51:27).

The cry ‘Remember me’ runs through Scripture. The psalms pray it; Hannah prays it; and on the cross a dying criminal says, “Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom!” (Luke 23:42).

Isaiah gives God's answer to everyone who feels forgotten: “Can a woman forget her nursing child, or lack compassion for the son of her womb?” And then: “Even if she could forget, I will not forget you!” (Isaiah 49:15).
passages.asks: Noah waited in the ark a long time with no word from God. Ask whether you are in a long wait right now, and whether you feel forgotten. God's remembering came before Noah could see dry land. Ask what it would mean to trust that you are remembered before you see the change.

passages.happening:
After forty more days Noah opens the window of the ark and sends out a raven. It keeps flying back and forth until the waters dry up (verses 6-7).

Then he sends out a dove. She finds “no place to rest her foot” and comes back, and Noah reaches out his hand and brings her inside (verses 8-9).

He waits seven more days and sends her again. This time she comes back in the evening “with a freshly plucked olive leaf in her beak.” Now Noah knows the waters have gone down (verses 10-11). He waits seven more days and sends her out once more, and she does not return (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The first hearers would know why the birds act as they do. A raven eats almost anything and can live without dry ground, so it simply stays out. A dove needs a place to perch and green things to eat. What the dove does tells Noah what he needs to know.

An olive tree does not grow on high mountains. A fresh olive leaf means the water has fallen low and plants are growing again.

The Babylonian flood story in the Epic of Gilgamesh has a scene very like this one. The flood hero, Utnapishtim, sends out a dove, which comes back, then a swallow, which comes back, then a raven, which does not. Genesis shares that picture with its world. But in Genesis the story is wrapped in God's remembering, and it leads not to a crowd of gods but to a promise.

Notice the tenderness in verse 9: Noah ‘reached out his hand and brought her back’. The man who was rescued rescues a small bird.
passages.later:
The dove comes back in the Gospels. When Jesus is baptized and comes up out of the water, he sees “the Spirit of God descending like a dove and resting on Him” (Matthew 3:16). Many Christians since the early church have heard an echo of Noah's dove over the waters. The New Testament does not draw that link, so it is best held as an echo, not a claim.

The waiting in these verses, seven days and then seven more, is the kind of waiting the psalms describe: “I wait for the LORD; my soul does wait, and in His word I put my hope” (Psalm 130:5).
passages.asks: Noah did not open the door the moment the rain stopped. He waited, and watched, and sent out the dove again. Ask whether you are rushing a season God has not yet finished. And look for the olive leaf: ask what small sign of new life God has already given you.

passages.happening:
In Noah's 601st year, on the first day of the first month, the waters have dried from the earth. Noah removes the covering of the ark and sees that the ground is dry (verse 13). By the twenty-seventh day of the second month, the earth is fully dry (verse 14).

Then God speaks: “Come out of the ark, you and your wife, along with your sons and their wives” (verse 16). Noah is to bring out all the living creatures “so that they can spread out over the earth and be fruitful and multiply upon it” (verse 17).

Noah comes out with his family, and every creature comes out, “kind by kind” (verses 18-19).
passages.hearers:
The dates matter. The flood began on the seventeenth day of the second month of Noah's 600th year (7:11). The earth is fully dry on the twenty-seventh day of the second month of the next year. Noah's family has been in the ark for about a year.

The new year begins with dry ground. The first day of the first month is a fresh start, a new creation. And the words God uses, ‘be fruitful and multiply’, are the words of the blessing in 1:22 and 1:28. The world is being given back.

Noah does not leave the ark when he sees dry ground. He waits until God tells him to come out. He went in at God's word, and he comes out at God's word.
passages.later:
Paul says that creation still groans, waiting to be made new: “the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until the present time” (Romans 8:22). The new start after the flood was real, but it was not the last one.

The Bible's last picture is a new creation without any flood: “Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and earth had passed away, and the sea was no more” (Revelation 21:1). In the Bible the sea often stands for chaos and danger. In the end it is gone.
passages.asks: Noah stepped out into a world that had been emptied. He had to begin again. Ask what it looks like to begin again after a loss, and whether you can hear God's word ‘be fruitful’ spoken over the ground that is left. And notice that Noah waited for God's word to come out. Ask whose word you are waiting on.

passages.happening:
The first thing Noah does is build an altar to the LORD. He takes some of every kind of clean animal and clean bird and offers “burnt offerings on the altar” (verse 20).

“When the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma, He said in His heart, ‘Never again will I curse the ground because of man, even though every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth. And never again will I destroy all living creatures as I have done’” (verse 21).

Then comes a short poem of promise: “As long as the earth endures, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night shall never cease” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
This is the first altar in the Bible. A ‘burnt offering’ (olah) was the whole animal burned on the altar, given entirely to God. It said: everything belongs to you.

‘Pleasing aroma’ is the phrase Israel's law uses for an offering God accepts (Leviticus 1:9). The word for ‘pleasing’ sounds like Noah's name and the word for rest. God's acceptance is pictured as rest after the storm.

The first hearers would know that other peoples told this scene differently. In Babylon's stories the gods relied on people's offerings for food. In the Gilgamesh flood story, when Utnapishtim makes his offering after the flood, the gods gather around it. In Genesis the LORD needs nothing. He receives Noah's worship and answers it with a promise.

The promise is surprising. Before the flood, God judged because ‘every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was altogether evil’ (6:5). Now he says nearly the same thing about the human heart, and promises never to send such a flood again. The flood did not change the human heart. God's patience is not based on people becoming good. It is based on his own mercy.
passages.later:
Paul uses the language of this offering for Christ's death: Christ “gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God” (Ephesians 5:2). Noah's offering was received, and God promised to bear with a sinful world. Christ's offering deals with the sin itself.

The prophets promise what the flood could not do. God says, “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26).

The steady seasons of verse 22 become a picture of God's faithfulness. Jeremiah speaks of God's covenant with the day and with the night (Jeremiah 33:20), and the psalm says, “You made the summer and winter” (Psalm 74:17). Every sunrise and every harvest is a kept promise.
passages.hard:
Why does God ‘smell’ the offering, as if he needed it? The Bible often speaks of God in human terms: he sees, hears, comes down, smells. These words help people understand that God truly receives worship and truly responds to it. They do not mean that God is hungry or needs anything from us. Genesis sets this scene beside stories in which the gods did depend on human offerings, and it quietly says the opposite.

Why does God promise not to judge again in this way, when people are no better? The text gives no reason in people. The reason is in God. His promise rests on his own choice to be patient, not on any change in the human heart. Christians read that patience as leaving room for a rescue that would come later, through Abraham's family and through Christ.
passages.asks: The first thing Noah did on dry ground was worship. Ask what your first act is when you come through a hard season. Then look at the seasons around you this week: seedtime, harvest, cold, heat, day and night. Ask whether you notice them as promises kept.
